column1: #mapping_set_title: "Lifted CelesTrak SATCAT vocabulary to Rovetto SSAO crosswalk"

#comment: "Candidate-for-review alignment between the lifted SATCAT operational vocabulary (70,122 instances) and the Space Situational Awareness Ontology (Rovetto, NASA mission-viz vendoring, 353 classes). Rows with predicate_modifier=Not are asserted NON-mappings. SKOS direction per the SKOS Reference: A skos:narrowMatch B asserts B is the narrower concept; A skos:broadMatch B asserts B is the broader concept. Every correspondence here is additionally subject to EXTENSIONAL testing against the instance data (gate/mutations.py): a mapping the reasoner cannot reject may still be refuted by the catalogue."

column9: Both denote the mission-carrying object a launch exists for. Not exact: SSAO also has Spacecraft_Payload for instruments carried aboard; the SATCAT PAY code is the whole spacecraft.
Every catalogued payload is an artificial satellite of some body; Artificial_Satellite is the broader concept, also covering objects SATCAT files elsewhere.

Catalogued R/B entries are spent stages, which SSAO files as a debris subclass. Edge honestly noted: a stage in active use during launch is not yet debris, but the catalogue's standing population is spent stages.
The catalogue DEB code is the on-orbit non-functional fragment population, SSAO's Orbital_Debris. Space_Debris is broader in SSAO (subsuming rocket and payload debris categories regardless of orbit).

Asserted non-mapping, the lexical trap of this pair: SATCAT DEB covers fragmentation debris AND mission-related debris (lens caps, separation hardware) which SSAO deliberately separates into MissionRelatedDebris. Equating DEB with Fragmentation_Debris silently misfiles every catalogued lens cap. The catalogue does not distinguish the two, so no extensional test can save this mapping either: it must be refused at curation time.
An unknown-type catalogue entry is still a resident space object; nothing narrower is safe to assert.

Status-to-class coercion, flagged: SATCAT '+' marks operational status of an object, SSAO Operational_Satellite is a satellite kind. The mapping holds only for payloads; an operational-status rocket body is not an Operational_Satellite. The harness tests exactly this edge.
Non-operational payloads are defunct spacecraft. Same status-to-class caveat as above; debris with '-' status is not a spacecraft.
Same threshold family: SSAO's own definition text names ~2000 km bounds for the LEO regime; our derivation uses apogee < 2000 km.
Between the LEO and GEO bands on both sides.
Period in the sidereal-day band (1400 to 1500 minutes) is the geosynchronous condition; inclination is unconstrained.
Geostationary candidates (period band plus inclination <= 5 degrees) are the narrower special case of geosynchronous.

Close, not exact, and threshold-dependent: true geostationary requires near-zero inclination AND near-circularity; our 5-degree candidate band over-approximates. The harness quantifies the over-approximation.
Super-synchronous disposal band above GEO; both sides mean the disposal region.
Large apogee-perigee gap is the defining property on both sides.

Asserted non-mapping: a decayed object has re-entered and is no longer resident in orbit. Mapping decayed entries to any resident-object or orbit class is the catalogue-scale false friend, and it is EXTENSIONALLY visible: every instance carries a decay date that contradicts residency. The harness counts exactly how visible.
All catalogued debris is artificial; the broader anchor holds for every object type in the catalogue.
